title: Meta-learning and recursive self-improvement
matchup: Bengio et al. (1991) and current meta-learning and self-improvement research vs Schmidhuber (1987, 1992, 2003)
question: Does Schmidhuber's 1987 thesis establish the priority he claims for algorithmic meta-learning and recursive self-improvement?

usual_credit.summary: Bengio said in a December 2019 IEEE Spectrum interview that he wrote an early paper on learning to learn in 1991, and Bengio, Bengio and Cloutier published "Learning a synaptic learning rule" at IJCNN that year. The idea that machines could improve themselves in an intelligence explosion is traced by Schmidhuber, and by commenters under his posts, to I. J. Good's "Speculations concerning the first ultraintelligent machine", published in Advances in Computers in 1966.

works.who: Yoshua Bengio, Samy Bengio and Jocelyn Cloutier
works.title: Learning a synaptic learning rule
Speculations concerning the first ultraintelligent machine (Advances in Computers, vol. 6)

claim.summary: Schmidhuber describes his 1987 diploma thesis as a concrete algorithm for recursive self-improvement: an evolutionary program improves learning procedures, including the procedure used to improve them, at successive meta levels. He contrasts this with Bengio's 1991 work and with earlier general predictions of an intelligence explosion. He also cites his later gradient-based meta-learning, self-modifying reinforcement learners and Gödel Machine as distinct developments. The priority he claims for the thesis is for an algorithmic formulation, not for originating every broad idea about machines improving themselves or every modern use of the term meta-learning.

Goedel machines: self-referential universal problem solvers making provably optimal self-improvements

quotes.text: Bengio, however, suggested in public at N(eur)IPS 2019 that he did it before me, citing his much later 1991 paper.
In 1987, when compute was 100,000,000 x more expensive, I published the 1st concrete RSI algorithms.
My 1987 diploma thesis [META1], however, applied "genetic programming" (GP) to itself, to recursively evolve better GP methods.
(Good did not have any concrete RSI algorithms)
My first work on metalearning or learning to learn came out in 1987 [1][2]. Back then nobody was interested.

response.summary: Bengio's 2019 IEEE Spectrum interview dates his early learning-to-learn paper to 1991, without addressing the 1987 thesis. An archived discussion reports a keynote slide citing Bengio et al. (1991) and Schmidhuber (1992), but the slide itself is not supplied with that account. Hinton's October 2026 post says recursive self-improvement and an intelligence explosion are old ideas, while Schmidhuber distinguishes Good's earlier speculation from a concrete algorithm. These sources document different conceptions of the contribution; they do not contain a direct technical rebuttal of the thesis's specific evolutionary procedure.

quotes.text: I wrote an early paper on this in 1991, but only recently did we get the computational power to implement this kind of thing.

quotes.who: Geoffrey Hinton (X, not addressed to Schmidhuber's claim)
quotes.text: The idea of an intelligence explosion caused by recursive self improvement has been around for a long time

agreed_facts: Schmidhuber's diploma thesis on learning how to learn is dated 1987 and was written at the Technical University of Munich.
Bengio, Bengio and Cloutier published "Learning a synaptic learning rule" at IJCNN in 1991, and Bengio dated his early paper on learning to learn to 1991 in a December 2019 interview.
I. J. Good wrote about an intelligence explosion through self-improving machines in 1965 to 1966, and Schmidhuber's own text says Good had no concrete recursive self-improvement algorithm.
Schmidhuber published the Gödel Machine in 2003, and he published the technical note "Recursive self-improvement since 1987" in September 2026.
crux: The sources differ on whether learning to learn and recursive self-improvement are best credited to the first concrete algorithm, which Schmidhuber places in 1987, or to later formulations, and on whether today's meta-learning, which trains across task distributions or works in context, is the same thing as the evolutionary system of the thesis. They also differ on whether Bengio's 1991 paper deserves to be named alongside the thesis.
